Eyes and attention: soft focus, hard focus and the quiet eye

A round of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting takes much longer than the shooting itself. You walk, wait and watch others; the shots take only a few seconds per target. Hardly anyone can hold full attention for all that time, and you do not need to.

Many coaches suggest treating attention like a switch. Between stands you switch off: talk, drink water, rest your eyes. About two or three minutes before your turn, you switch on again.

Coaches' experience

When your head is tired from long, hard thinking, your aim can get worse; this has been seen in archery, for example. So adding up scores or scrolling your phone for a long time between stands may tire you more than you expect.

Some research

During the target presentation, use your attention to plan. Where does the target come from, where do you see it clearly, where will you break it? This gives you the pick-up point, the hold point and the break point: see Three points: pick-up, hold and break. When Compak® Sporting is shot by squad, only the day's first squad watches a demonstration, early in the morning (Chapter 17 · Squad: showing the targets). Later squads learn the targets by watching the shooters before them, unless a stop of more than 10 minutes brings a new demonstration of the singles.

Coaches' experience

Focus: a soft focus, calm and wide, while your eyes wait at the pick-up point; then a hard focus on the target itself, often its leading edge. Some shooters look back at the barrel or the bead (the small dot at the muzzle end of the rib) to check their lead. Lead is how far in front of the target you point the gun, and checking it this way often makes the gun slow down or stop.

Coaches' experience

The barrels stay at the edge of your vision. Experienced shooters often say they hardly notice the gun during the shot, because their eyes are on the target.

Coaches' experience

Researchers call the last steady look before a movement the quiet eye. In studies across many sports, more skilled performers tend to start it earlier and hold it longer, and it is often longer on successful attempts than on failed ones.

Well researched

There is no set number of milliseconds to hold. For you it simply means: see the target early and keep your eyes on it while the gun moves smoothly. This has not been studied in Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting itself; most likely it works the same way there.

Coaches' experience

Attention is often pulled away by thoughts, not by the target: “what if I miss”, “how many have I dropped”. Worry takes attention away from the task, especially under pressure. One process goal, such as “see the front edge”, gives your attention a job: see Process goals and the score.

Some research

Attention can be trained: short rounds with a clear routine, practice with small distractions, and drills in which you follow moving things with your eyes. If your attention drifts after several rounds, that is normal tiredness; a short break helps more than forcing yourself.

Coaches' experience

Key points

  • Attention is a switch: on at the stand, off between stands.
  • Use the target presentation to choose the pick-up, hold and break points.
  • Soft focus before the call, hard focus on the target once it appears.
  • One process goal instead of thoughts about the score.
  • The quiet eye means seeing the target early and keeping your eyes on it; there is no set number of milliseconds.

Did you know?

Some coaches suggest a test for hard focus: try to see the rim or small details of the clay as it flies. If you can, your eyes are on the target, not on the gun.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. How can you manage your attention during a round?

    1. Keep full concentration the whole time
    2. On at the stand, off between stands
    3. Count your score after each target
    Answer

    On at the stand, off between stands

    Hardly anyone holds full attention for long; switch it on for the seconds when it matters.

  2. Where do your eyes go in hard focus?

    1. To the bead on the rib
    2. To the end of the barrels
    3. To the target itself
    Answer

    To the target itself

    Your eyes stay on the target, often its leading edge; the barrels and bead stay at the edge of your vision.

  3. What does research across many sports say about the quiet eye?

    1. Skilled performers tend to start it earlier and hold it longer
    2. It must last a fixed number of milliseconds
    3. It matters only in rifle and pistol shooting
    Answer

    Skilled performers tend to start it earlier and hold it longer

    Across many sports the final steady look tends to start earlier and last longer in skilled performers and on successful attempts, but there is no universal number to aim for.
